body:
## Overview
Yes. TTLCache.get still returns a value when the age is exactly ttl; it expires only when strictly older than ttl.

## How it works
put() stores (value, clock()) at cache.py:13. get() computes age = clock() - stored and expires on `age > ttl` (cache.py:20); expired entries are deleted and `default` returned (21-22). Otherwise the value is returned (23).

## Why it is this way
Direct: commit e6ed919 "Keep cache entries through their last second (#12)" (Ana) changed `>=` to `>`. Message: "On coarse clocks (time.monotonic on some platforms ticks in 15 ms steps) entries stored with ttl=1 expired on the first read after a one-tick advance. Serve an entry until it is strictly older than ttl, so ttl is the minimum lifetime callers can rely on." The original bdf7b91 (Sam) used `>=`. Searched: git log/blame on cache.py (only two commits); no tests or docs in the repo.

## Evidence
fake clock, ttl=10: age 10 -> "v"; age 10.001 -> "MISS". git blame -L 20,20 -> e6ed919.

## Gotchas
The class docstring (cache.py:5) says entries "expire after ttl seconds", which reads as expiry at ttl; actual behavior is ttl is a minimum lifetime, expiry just after.
